A3 terms
Acceptance

Allowing present inner experience without making its removal a condition for action.

In ACT, acceptance means making room for thoughts, feelings, or sensations while choosing how to act. It does not mean approving harm, abandoning boundaries, or giving up on change.

Category:

See also

  • Psychological Flexibility
  • Willingness

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapters 4 and 9

Learn more (1)

  • Making Room for Experience
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy

Also called: ACT

An approach that supports flexible, values-guided action alongside difficult inner experiences.

ACT develops ways to notice thoughts and feelings, make room for them when useful, and act in personally meaningful directions. Its aim is greater flexibility, rather than eliminating every uncomfortable thought or feeling.

Category:

See also

  • Acceptance
  • Cognitive Defusion
  • Psychological Flexibility
  • Values

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Introduction; Chapters 4-13

Learn more (1)

  • Making Room for Experience
Automatic Thought

Also called: Automatic Thoughts

A thought or mental image that arises without deliberate effort.

Automatic thoughts are quick interpretations of a situation. Noticing one allows you to examine its accuracy and usefulness instead of treating it as an established fact.

Category:

See also

  • Cognitive Model
  • Core Belief

References

  • Beck Institute: Cognitive Model

Learn more (1)

  • Working with Anger, Guilt & Shame
B2 terms
Behavioural Activation

Also called: Behavioral Activation

Planning manageable activities that support engagement with daily life.

Behavioural activation works with the cycle of low mood and reduced activity. Choose achievable actions connected to care, connection, enjoyment, or accomplishment, and notice what happens rather than waiting for motivation to arrive first.

Category:

See also

  • Values

References

  • Mind Over Mood, Second Edition: Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky, Chapter 13, pp. 188-218

Learn more (2)

  • Behaviour Activation
  • Maintaining Progress
Behavioural Experiment

Also called: Behavioral Experiment, Behavioral Experiments, Behavioural Experiments

A planned activity used to test a prediction.

A behavioural experiment compares what you expect with what actually happens. The result provides evidence to reconsider a belief.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Core Belief

References

  • Beck Institute: Cognitive Model

Learn more (1)

  • Assumptions & Core Beliefs
C5 terms
Cognitive Behavioural Therapy

Also called: CBT, Cognitive Behavior Therapy, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, Cognitive Behaviour Therapy

A therapy that works with patterns in thinking and behaviour.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy combines cognitive and behavioural approaches. It helps people examine interpretations and try different actions, rather than assuming that a distressing thought must be true.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Cognitive Model

References

  • APA Dictionary of Psychology: cognitive behavior therapy

Learn more (1)

  • Introduction to CBT
Cognitive Defusion

Also called: Defusion

Noticing a thought as a thought rather than automatically obeying it.

Defusion changes your relationship to thinking. You can notice a prediction or self-judgment and choose your response without having to prove the thought false or force it to stop.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Self-as-Context

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapter 6, pp. 69-86

Learn more (1)

  • Thoughts & the Observing Perspective
Cognitive Model

An account of how interpretations influence feelings, body responses, and actions.

The cognitive model connects a situation with its personal meaning and the responses that follow. Beliefs shape those interpretations; examining them can reveal other ways of understanding the situation.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Core Belief

References

  • Beck Institute: Cognitive Model
Committed Action

Taking and reviewing practical steps guided by your values.

Committed action turns a valued direction into behaviour. It includes adjusting plans after obstacles and beginning again, rather than demanding perfect persistence with a plan that no longer fits.

Category:

See also

  • Values
  • Willingness

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapter 13, pp. 177-194

Learn more (1)

  • Values & Committed Action
Core Belief

Also called: Core Beliefs

A broad belief about yourself, other people, or the world.

Core beliefs influence how you interpret experiences. In CBT, identifying and examining an unhelpful belief can support more balanced conclusions.

Category:

See also

  • Automatic Thought
  • Cognitive Model

References

  • Beck Institute: Cognitive Model

Learn more (2)

  • Assumptions & Core Beliefs
  • Working with Anger, Guilt & Shame
D1 terms
Dialectical Behaviour Therapy

Also called: DBT, Dialectical Behavior Therapy, Dialectical Behavioral Therapy, Dialectical Behavioural Therapy

A therapy that combines behavioural change methods with mindfulness and acceptance.

Dialectical Behaviour Therapy brings together behavioural approaches and mindfulness. DBT skills training teaches practical ways to manage distress, emotions, attention, and relationships; a skills website is only one educational resource, not a complete DBT treatment programme.

Category:

See also

  • Mindfulness
  • Wise Mind

References

  • APA Dictionary of Psychology: dialectical behavior therapy
E1 terms
Emotion Mind

A state in which feelings and urges strongly guide your response.

Emotion Mind gives priority to emotional information. Other facts or longer-term goals can become harder to consider.

Category:

See also

  • Reasonable Mind
  • Wise Mind

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition: Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 3: Wise Mind - States of Mind
H1 terms
HOW Skills

The qualities Non-Judgmentally, One-Mindfully, and Effectively.

HOW Skills describe how to practise a WHAT skill. These qualities can be used together.

  • WHAT Skills

M1 terms
Mindfulness

Awareness of present experience with openness and acceptance.

Mindfulness means deliberately noticing current experience without immediately judging or pushing it away. It can be practised during everyday activities, not only meditation.

Category:

See also

  • HOW Skills
  • WHAT Skills
  • Wise Mind

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition: Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 1A: Mindfulness Definitions

Learn more (1)

  • Thoughts & the Observing Perspective
P1 terms
Psychological Flexibility

The ability to respond to the present situation in ways that serve your values.

Psychological flexibility combines awareness and openness with useful action. It includes changing course when needed instead of letting rigid rules or attempts to avoid every uncomfortable feeling determine your choices.

Category:

See also

  • Acceptance
  • Cognitive Defusion
  • Committed Action

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Introduction; Chapters 4-13

Learn more (1)

  • Making Room for Experience
R1 terms
Reasonable Mind

A state that prioritizes facts, logic, and practical tasks.

Reasonable Mind approaches situations analytically. Used alone, it may overlook feelings, needs, or values.

Category:

See also

  • Emotion Mind
  • Wise Mind

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition: Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 3: Wise Mind - States of Mind
S1 terms
Self-as-Context

Also called: Observing Self

The perspective from which you notice changing thoughts, feelings, and experiences.

In ACT, self-as-context involves noticing experience without reducing your identity to one thought, feeling, role, or story. It does not require becoming detached or losing contact with the present situation.

Category:

See also

  • Cognitive Defusion
  • Mindfulness

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapter 7, pp. 87-104

Learn more (1)

  • Thoughts & the Observing Perspective
U1 terms
Underlying Assumption

Also called: Underlying Assumptions

A personal rule or prediction that guides how you respond.

An underlying assumption connects a condition with an expected result, such as expecting rejection whenever you disagree. Treating the rule as a testable prediction can reveal where it fits and where it is too rigid.

Category:

See also

  • Behavioural Experiment
  • Core Belief

References

  • Mind Over Mood, Second Edition: Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky, Chapter 11, pp. 132-151

Learn more (1)

  • Assumptions & Core Beliefs
V1 terms
Values

Chosen qualities you want to bring to your ongoing actions.

Values describe how you want to act, such as with care or curiosity. A goal can be completed; a value can guide many different actions over time.

Category:

See also

  • Committed Action

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapters 11-12, pp. 153-176

W3 terms
WHAT Skills

The mindfulness actions Observe, Describe, and Participate.

WHAT Skills identify what you do while practising mindfulness. Choose one action to focus on at a time.

Category:

See also

  • HOW Skills
  • Mindfulness

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition: Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 4: Taking Hold of Your Mind - What Skills

Willingness

Readiness to experience discomfort when it accompanies a meaningful action.

Willingness concerns what you are prepared to make room for, not whether you enjoy it. It can support an achievable step toward a value without requiring anxiety or uncertainty to disappear first.

Category:

See also

  • Acceptance
  • Committed Action

References

  • Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life: Steven C. Hayes with Spencer Smith, Chapters 9-10, pp. 121-152

Learn more (2)

  • Making Room for Experience
  • Values & Committed Action
Wise Mind

Wise Mind is the integrated perspective that draws on both emotion and reason.

Wise Mind is a DBT concept for the integrated perspective that draws on both emotional experience and reasonable thinking. It supports noticing what is true, what matters, and what an effective next step may be.

Category:

References

  • DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition: Marsha M. Linehan, Mindfulness Handout 3: Wise Mind - States of Mind
